blocks.text: Chapter 3.
How Superforecasters Think: Fermi-ize and Zoom Out
Third night, friend — and we open the toolbox at last. But first, a classroom in Chicago, decades ago, where a physicist is asking his students a question that cannot possibly be answered:
"How many piano tuners are there in Chicago?"

No phone book allowed. No data. The students stare. And Enrico Fermi — the man who built the first nuclear reactor — smiles, because he knows something they don't: the impossible question is just several possible questions wearing a trench coat.
The watchmaker's method

Watch Fermi take the question apart. How many people in Chicago? — about 2.5 million, that's known. People per household? Fraction of households with a regularly tuned piano? — maybe one in a hundred, plus schools and halls. Tunings per piano per year? — roughly one. Tunings one tuner can do in a year? — perhaps a thousand. Multiply, divide... and you land in the low sixties. The Chicago phone book at one point listed about eighty. From nothing — no data, no lookup — to within throwing distance of truth.

The technique is called Fermi-izing, and its power is double. First, each sub-estimate can err in either direction, so the errors partially cancel instead of compounding. Second — more important — decomposition flushes hidden assumptions into the open, where they can be examined and fixed. The alternative — answering from the gut — is the tip-of-your-nose again: it feels like insight, and it's just whatever System 1 happened to serve. Superforecasters do this reflexively, friend: where ordinary minds see one giant unanswerable question and freeze, they see a bundle of tractable pieces — some researchable, some boundable — and even crude bounds on each piece beat one crude guess at the whole.
The Arafat question
Now watch the method under fire. In 2012, tournament forecasters faced a genuinely bizarre question: would Swiss scientists find elevated polonium in the exhumed remains of Yasser Arafat?

Most people instantly answered a different question — the emotional one: "Did Israel poison Arafat?" — attribute substitution striking again, and fatally, because the two questions have different answers.
Pause and guess: Superforecaster Bill Flack refused the swap and Fermi-ized the question as actually worded. What sub-questions did he find — and what was the subtle insight that set his probability?
Ready? Here is what happened.

First: can polonium even be detected a decade after death? It decays fast — this took real research, which showed detection remained possible. Second: would the testing actually proceed? And third — the masterstroke — how many distinct pathways lead to "yes"? Israel might have poisoned him. Someone else might have. Or polonium might have been planted on the remains after death to frame Israel. Three independent roads to "elevated polonium found" — which means the probability of "yes" was higher than any single poisoning theory alone would suggest. Flack forecast about 60% yes... and the Swiss team duly reported elevated polonium. The lesson, friend, is unglamorous and decisive: unpack the question as posed, not the question your emotions want to answer. A question about test results is not a question about guilt; a question about a leader leaving office is not a question about whether you like him. List every pathway to each outcome — especially the ones that have nothing to do with your pet theory.
Meet the Renzettis

Now the second tool, and a family you'll never forget. The Renzettis: modest house, Frank's a bookkeeper, Mary works part-time at a daycare, one child, saving for college. Question: what's the chance they own a pet?

Almost everyone dives into the details — tight budget, small house, busy lives. Superforecasters ask a different question first: what percentage of American households own a pet? About 62%. That's the base rate — the outside view: treat the case as an instance of a class before treating it as unique. Only then switch to the inside view and adjust for the particulars.

And the order is everything, friend, because of a force you met in the Ariely nights: anchoring. The first number you touch pulls every later adjustment toward it — even a rigged wheel of fortune drags estimates. You will anchor on something; the only choice is what. Start with the inside view and you anchor on a vivid detail; start with the outside view and you anchor on reality's average. Applied to geopolitics: "will there be a lethal Sino-Japanese clash this year?" begins not with this week's furious headlines but with history — how often have comparable standoffs turned lethal per year? The base rate rarely gives the final answer. But it stops the final answer from floating free of all historical experience — and skipping it is the single most common amateur error in forecasting.
The ox and the dragonfly

Plymouth, England, 1906. A livestock fair. Nearly 800 fairgoers pay to guess the weight of an ox, and the statistician Francis Galton collects the tickets, expecting to demonstrate the ignorance of crowds.
Pause and guess: The ox weighed 1,198 pounds. What was the crowd's collective guess — and what does the gap explain?
Ready? Here is what happened.

1,197 pounds. Off by one — closer than any individual, including the cattle experts. The logic became famous as the wisdom of crowds: every judgment mixes genuine information with error, and when many independent judgments combine, the errors — scattered in all directions — cancel, while the information accumulates. Superforecasters internalize this as the dragonfly eye: a dragonfly's compound eye holds thousands of lenses fused into one image, and the best forecasters deliberately hunt perspectives that clash with their own — hostile commentators, rival framings, contrary analysts — and synthesize them, rather than finding one congenial view and stopping. And here is the delightful twist, friend: you can crowd-source inside your own skull. Researchers Vul and Pashler found that averaging two estimates from the same person — the second made after a delay, or after being told "assume your first answer is wrong; why?" — beats either estimate alone. The crowd within. So after every judgment: assume it's mistaken, spend five minutes on the strongest reason why, and average. Flip the question — "what's the chance this doesn't happen?" — and watch information surface that the first pass missed.
Open minds beat high IQs

So are these people simply geniuses? The data says no — and it's the most encouraging finding in the book. Regular tournament forecasters tested around the 70th percentile in intelligence; superforecasters around the 80th — above average, nowhere near Einstein, and plenty of higher-IQ participants forecast worse. Beyond a decent threshold, raw brainpower buys little. What you have matters less than how you use it.

The trait that actually discriminates is what psychologist Jonathan Baron calls active open-mindedness: treating beliefs as testable hypotheses rather than treasures to defend — actively hunting evidence against your own views, and scoring a changed mind as a win, not a defeat. Superforecasters score distinctly high. It's the fox-over-hedgehog result seen at the level of a single skull: the hedgehog deploys intelligence as a lawyer defending One Big Idea; the fox deploys it as an investigator integrating many small ones. And the implication, friend, is the whole reason this book is on the shelf: the style is learnable. Fermi-izing, base-rate anchoring, dragonfly aggregation — procedures, not talents. This week: take one hard question, break it into five pieces, write the base rate down first, and read one source you expect to disagree with. That's the apprenticeship.
Before you go

So: impossible questions are possible questions in a trench coat; answer what was asked, not what your feelings substitute; anchor on reality's average before the vivid details; fuse contrary lenses like a dragonfly — including the second opinion hiding in your own head; and know that the crown goes not to the highest IQ but to the most open mind.

But a puzzle remains, friend. Once you've decomposed, anchored, and aggregated... you must still commit to a number. And here superforecasters do something that sounds almost absurd: they distinguish 63% from 65% — and it matters. Tomorrow: why probability comes in finer grain than "maybe"; the three-setting mental dial most humans never escape; and what a president's advisers meant when they told him an invasion plan was a "fair chance" — right before the Bay of Pigs.
Next time: the fine art of maybe.
Key takeaways
Fermi-ize: break the impossible question into estimable pieces — errors cancel, and hidden assumptions surface for inspection.
Answer the question as posed: Flack's polonium forecast counted every pathway to "yes," not just the emotionally loaded one.
Outside view first: you will anchor on something, so anchor on the base rate — reality's average — before adjusting for details.
The dragonfly eye: hunt clashing perspectives and synthesize; Galton's crowd beat every expert by letting errors cancel.
Use the crowd within: assume your judgment is wrong, argue why, and average the two views.
Superforecasting is a stance, not a gift: active open-mindedness — beliefs as hypotheses under test — beats raw IQ.
